title: Looking back: the practices
hookLine: metta, breath, walking, precepts, giving, the holy days

lines: A YEAR LATER, TALKING ABOUT DINNER.
cards: A new driver grips the wheel with both hands and says each step under her breath: mirror, signal, look. Every turn is a small exam. A year later she merges onto the highway while talking about dinner.
She doesn't remember the lessons. Her hands just know. Something like that can happen with a year of practice.
The practices came one at a time, often a little clumsily. Somewhere along the way, some of them may have stopped being lessons and started being things you do.

teach.h: METTA — FROM YOURSELF TO ALL BEINGS.

teach.b: Four phrases wishing safety and ease, first to yourself, then to a benefactor, a dear friend, a neutral person, a difficult one, and finally to all beings, as the metta sutta puts it, like a mother protecting her only child.
The breath. Sixteen steps of breathing mindfully: knowing the long breath and the short one, the whole body, joy and ease, the mind, and change. Counting when the mind is busy.
Naming the hindrances when they arrive. Walking. A short lane, lifting, moving, placing, and the turn at the end, where you notice the wanting to turn before you turn.
Walking in the city, too. The precepts. The three refuges and the five training rules: not killing, not taking, care in sex, true speech, a clear mind.
And when you break one: notice, make amends, begin again. Giving. Giving first, before you feel ready.
The giver who is glad three times: before, while, and after. The poor woman's lamp that burned longest.
Giving attention, and giving without a receipt.

The holy days. The full and new moons of the uposatha, Vesak and the baby Buddha's bath, lanterns on the water, the rains retreat, and Kathina, when the robes are given. That's a lot, and nobody keeps all of it every day.
The point was never to collect practices. It was to find the few that fit your life, and let them become what your hands already know.

how: Lay Buddhists typically build a few practices into ordinary life: metta and breath meditation, walking meditation, keeping the five precepts, giving to monasteries and others, and keeping the moon days and festivals of their tradition.

o: a checklist to keep every practice daily
the year's practices, now part of your days
a test of how well you meditate now

games.q: match each practice from the year.

s: a good practitioner keeps every practice every day
nobody does; the point is to find the few that fit your life.
metta starts with wishing yourself well
then a benefactor, a dear friend, a neutral person, a difficult one, and all beings.
when you break a precept, the path says to give up
notice, make amends, and begin again.

games.q: you're giving something to someone. the Buddha says a giver can be glad three times. when?
games.why: glad before giving, glad while giving, glad after: the gladness doesn't depend on thanks or return.

practice: Take a quick tour: one silent metta phrase for yourself, may I be at ease; three slow steps, lifting, moving, placing; one small precept held in mind for the next hour; and one thing you could give today.
Then sit, and let the breath be the whole practice, long or short, just as it is. Another day, each of these can have a full minute of its own.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. Metta, the breath, walking, the precepts, giving and the holy days: the practices of the year, now yours to keep.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit bhāvanā: cultivation, bringing into being; the usual word for meditation and practice.

carryVoice: Your line: you practice now. The few that fit your life are enough. Day three hundred twenty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.37 (the giver glad three times)
